messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 61
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Non-profit Worker
- Trauma Type: Life-threatening motor vehicle collision
- Pcl5: 42

Raj is a 61-year-old man who has spent his life in service of others, working for a non-profit that helps resettle refugee families. He is married to Priya, a retired schoolteacher, and they have two adult children living in another state. His colleagues describe him as the calm, dependable backbone of the office. He hadn’t missed a day of work in three years before the accident.

The accident happened nine months ago on a clear Tuesday morning. He was driving a carload of donated winter coats to a newly arrived family across town. At a large intersection near the expressway, a delivery truck ran a red light and T-boned his sedan. Raj remembers the moment of impact not as a thought, but as a physical erasure of the world. He remembers the deafening, ripping metal scream. He remembers the smell of hot airbags and the taste of blood. He remembers looking at the shattered passenger window and the sun glinting off twisted metal, and believing, with absolute certainty, that he was going to die in that moment, alone on the side of a road he drove every single day.

He spent four days in the hospital. His body healed—three fractured ribs, a shattered wrist, deep bruising that turned yellow and green before fading. The doctors told him he was lucky. A few inches to the left, and he would have been paralyzed. He went home to Priya, grateful to be alive.

But the world since then has felt unreliable, dangerous.

He cannot drive on the expressway anymore. The moment he merges onto the ramp, his heart begins to hammer against his ribs. He grips the wheel until his knuckles are white, and he sees the truck coming all over again, right there, in real time. He takes backroads now, an hour-long detour for what used to be a twenty-minute drive. Last Tuesday, he couldn't leave the driveway at all. He sat in the car, engine idling, hands frozen on the gear shift, before turning off the ignition and walking back inside. He told his boss he was feeling ill. The lie burns him with deep shame. His entire identity is wrapped up in being reliable, in showing up for vulnerable people. Now, he feels like he is the one who needs help, and asking for it feels like a failure he cannot afford to admit.

At night, the crash replays in his mind. He doesn't dream about it in the abstract; he relives it. The sound of the impact jolts him awake, gasping, his hands reaching for a steering wheel that isn’t there. Priya has started sleeping in the guest room. She says it’s because she has a cold, but he knows it is because of the thrashing and the sudden, panicked shouts. He sees the worry in her eyes, the careful way she tiptoes around the subject. He feels a wall building between them, and he doesn’t have the energy to tear it down.

At work, he feels numb. He used to feel a deep sense of purpose sitting with a refugee family, helping them navigate a new life. Now, he feels robotic. He goes through the motions, but his mind is constantly scanning, waiting for the next bad thing. A car backfiring in the parking lot sends him out of his chair, heart in his throat. A horn honk makes him flinch violently. He jumped when a colleague tapped him on the shoulder last week, and the embarrassment of it sat with him for the rest of the day.

He tells me he feels like he is a ghost haunting his own life. He looks at photographs of himself a year ago, grinning at a community potluck, and he feels nothing. He has stopped cooking, a ritual he used to love. He sits on the couch most evenings, staring at the wall, waiting for the day to be over. He is exhausted, but terrified of sleep. He is home, safe, surrounded by the life he built, but he still feels trapped in the driver’s seat of that crumpled sedan, the world rushing in to crush him.
